[Dedication to CLO Coffee ☕️ — Acrostic Poem 001, Ode Poem 001 & Limerick Poem 001]

⸻

☕️ A C R O S T I C  P O E M — “BE KiND”

Calma en taza, aroma que eleva.
Luz entre sombras, donde el alma se renueva.
Obra divina, café que predica paz.

Confianza líquida, abrazo de mañana.
Ojos despiertos, corazones que sanan.
Fuego suave que inspira sin quemar.
Fortaleza y fe en cada sorbo al despertar.
Energía pura, alquimia del bien.
En cada trago, el alma dice: Amén.

⸻

🥄 L I M E R I C K  P O E M — “THE CUP THAT SMILES BACK”

There once was a brew at C-L-O,
That melted the frost in my soul.
With beans from afar, they raised the bar—
And “Be Kind” became their goal. ☕️✨

⸻

❤️ O D E  T O  C L O  C O F F E E — “THE ALTAR OF KINDNESS”

Oh CLO, temple of roasted dreams,
where hearts slow down and moments steam.
Ralph and Jen, architects of serenity,
your kindness drips through each pour-over.

In your corner of this wild world, kindness has a flavor—
the first sip that forgives the morning,
the last drop that blesses the night.

Your motto “BE KiND” is communion, not branding—
love in liquid form.

As Odd Mobb’s Left to Right loops for the 33rd time,
I remember—ten years ago from TODAY 10/11/2016 —‘FMMSHOTME’was born.
Yesterday reborn as @ojosdefmmshotme—
proof that art and caffeine never sleep.

So here’s to @odd_mob @starting5nick and every late-night edit.
Let this be my testament:

☕️ Be kind to all that breathe.
☕️ Make this life worth living.
☕️ Be immortal through intention and creation.

Thank you Ralph & Jen for divinity in a cup.
God bless your hands, your beans, your hearts.

Amen. Amén.

Frankie’s Restaurant. Arthur Avenue and E 186th Street. What to say about Frankie’s? It’s a classic kind of old-school, red-sauce, Italian-American, howyoudoin-fugedabowdit, kind of place. It was completely empty when I went for lunch, (to be expected at 1pm on a weekday). The menu isn’t massive, which I like, featuring all the typical Italian dishes you would expect in a place like this. My waitress was quick and nice, she recommended Chicken alla Vodka which came with penne. I can’t complain about the food at all, it was very much solid. I took a peak at the cocktail menu and I wasn’t impressed, (muddling a cherry and orange in an old fashioned?? In 2025??). I went with a glass of house red, which was very much serviceable. The food was $33 and the wine was $15, definitely on the pricey side but not completely outrageous. All in all, I’d give Frankie’s an 8.6/10. It’s not somewhere I’d cross two Burroughs to get to, but if you’re in the area and want a pretty good Italian place, Frankie’s is your spot.

Final thoughts: 

Finally made my way up to the Bronx! 

Arthur Avenue is the "Little Italy" of the Bronx, and it came with so many recommendations from my colleagues that I had to travel there for myself! We tried out Casa Della Mozzarella, and whoa, that restaurant was PACKED! Lines out the door and down the street too which made us excited to see what all the hype was about! 

The sub we got was HUGE and well worth the price! Each ingredient got its chance to shine through. The bun was tough and crunchy, providing a stable base to the food. The prosciutto was soft and wonderfully savory. The mozzarella had a fantastic soft texture and strong flavor, making it the highlight of the sandwich for sure! It also had pesto and sun dried peppers that rounded out the sub. 

Such a fun restaurant to go to! Absolutely stuffed full of food and people (suuuper skinny space inside too...you have been warned), this deli is peak "NYC deli", and I loved it! Well worth the trip to the Bronx to try it out!

A common question we see from Excel power users 👇
 “Can I create dependent dropdowns in monday.com like Excel?”
Here’s the expert answer:
❌ NOT THAT:
 Trying to recreate true Excel-style dynamic dropdowns.
 monday.com doesn’t currently support dropdown options that change dynamically based on another column’s value, and forcing it leads to messy data and fragile setups.
✅ DO THIS (the expert approach):
 Design around the platform using proven patterns:
• Use a category column (Fruits / Vegetables)
 • Use automations to clear or reset the second column when the category changes
 • Or split into separate columns (Fruit Type / Vegetable Type) and show or hide them with automations
 • If data is collected via Forms, use conditional logic to show the correct dropdown automatically
The result?
 ✔ Clean data
 ✔ Fewer mistakes
 ✔ A system that scales instead of breaking

caption:
Chuleton (txuleta in Basque Country) is the Spanish take on bone-in ribeye. At @bazaarmeatnewyork, by @chefjoseandres, they do it with Akaushi beef (a prized Kumamoto brown breed, raised in TX). Cooked over high heat on the @josperofficial to medium-rare, the meat shows up with charred crust and juicy interior. A superb steak! 

Yesterday, I raved about José's Taco, a delightful melange of nori & jamon & caviar & quail. The steak is a simpler dish, but equally delicious and similarly built around premium ingredients. The quality theme runs across the tasting menu. 

Here's the second half of the great tasting menu [first half posted yesterday]: 
- Bluefin Tuna and Fried Egg* chu-toro sashimi, quail eggs, soy 
- A5 "Philly Cheesesteak" with japanese beef, Manchego cheese espuma, caramelized onion jam
- the ribeye 
- seasonal mushroom with a rich garlic-chicken jus & egg yolk
- Buttered Potato Purée (lots of butter) 
- Key Lime Beach: key lime mousse, graham cracker cramble, lime 

We thoroughly enjoyed all we ate in this big space on the second floor of the @ritzcarltonnewyorknomad. The kitchen is open and dramatic. There's also plenty of table side cooking. It's a steakhouse, sort of - you could go and just get the ribeye - but also much more. Go get the tasting menu: kinda wacky, lots of fun, yummy. I'm a fan! 

#ribeye #chuleton #txuleta #リブロースステーキ #akaushi

location.name: Bazaar Meat by José Andrés, New York

caption:
José's Taco: jamón ibérico de bellota, ossetra caviar, quail egg, nori - a delightfully extravagant combo of big flavors & many textures. They harmonize. The nori adds nutty, grassy notes to all the protein feels. It's clever, fun, yummy. That's how I feel about the whole tasting menu experience at @bazaarmeatnewyork, by @chefjoseandres. 

Chef Andres is a superstar, who now has 40 restaurants. That scope could make me skeptical, but I thoroughly enjoyed this place, as I did @txulasteak last month. He clearly hires good people and thinks thing through. 

Here's the first half of the tasting menu: 
- Marinated "Ferran Adrià Liquid Olive with piparra peppers
- Caviar Cone with horseradish crème fraiche, chives, ossetra caviar, gold leaf
- José's Taco
- Cotton Candy Foie Gras crispy corn nuts
- Applewood Smoked shigoku Oysters with apple mignonette
- Neptune's Pillow: blue fin tuna, rocoto pepper, sesame, wasabi
- The Bazaar "Caesar" Salad prepared tableside, with gem leaves, idiazábal cheese, jamón crisp
[more later]

It's a big space, on the second floor of the @ritzcarltonnewyorknomad. Downstairs feels nightclubby, so the restaurant is calm by comparison - but there's a drama in all the food. It works. It's distinctive and special. I'm a fan!

caption:
On Friday, I had the immense pleasure of meeting @chefjoseandres . It was a truly inspiring experience, as Chef Jose is one of the main reasons I founded Cooks Who Feed.

His philosophy that most problems can be solved with simple solutions, to leverage those around you already doing the work, and not to wait for governments and NGOs, but to “change the recipe” ourselves, deeply resonated with me. I kept these principles in mind when I started Cooks Who Feed.

For me, the “simple solution” was the apron—a fundamental tool for cooks, chefs, and the hospitality industry. I noticed a gap in kitchenware, with no company focusing on both sustainability and social responsibility. I also saw amazing food charities that needed support. We didn’t invent the apron, but we certainly made it better by changing the recipe.

Thank you @chefjoseandres for all that you do and for being such a profound source of inspiration.

From barn to ballroom. 🐑🥂It’s hard to believe, but one of the most glamorous restaurants in NYC used to be a sheepfold.

For Day 23 of 25 Days of Christmas in NYC we are warming up at the legendary Tavern on the Green.

Built in 1870, this Victorian Gothic landmark was originally the “Sheepfold”—the actual home for the 200+ sheep that grazed in Central Park’s Sheep Meadow during the day! 

It wasn’t converted into a restaurant until 1934, but the historic stone architecture remains.

Today, it is a holiday icon and many are surprised by the building’s history. The courtyard is wrapped in thousands of lights and anchored by a massive Christmas tree. Whether you grab a dinner reservation or just sip a hot chocolate in the courtyard, it gives you that classic “Old New York” feeling.

Location: Central Park West & 67th St (Inside the park)

We were honored to welcome Kenta Watanabe, @watanabes_japan, one of the last remaining Japanese aishi and indigo producers, to share his practice. Kenta works with sukumo indigo using time-honored methods, carrying forward generations of Japanese dye knowledge. 

WSNF Trustee and shibori extraordinaire David Salama, @dsalama0, led participants through hands-on instruction throughout the workshop.

World Shibori Network is proud to offer exclusive U.S. access to Kenta Watanabe’s indigo kits, available only through WSN and North Folk House @northfolkhouse.

A huge thank you to Nancy Adler for joining us and capturing the community and spirit of this event through her stunning photography.

Tavern on the Green is not just a restaurant — it’s a landmark steeped in history, a jewel of Central Park, and a classic New York gathering place. What makes it truly special is its setting, its legacy, and its enduring place in the city’s cultural story.

Since opening as a restaurant in 1934, Tavern on the Green has become woven into the fabric of New York life — a place where generations have gathered to celebrate, reflect, and simply be part of the city.

The building itself carries an even deeper history. Long before it became a restaurant, it began life in the 1870s as a sheepfold, housing the sheep that once grazed on Sheep Meadow. It was designed by one of Central Park’s original architects, linking it directly to the park’s earliest vision.

Today, Tavern on the Green stands as a living reminder that New York’s past and present often meet in the most beautiful places — right in the heart of the park 🌿
